newsitem.title: USA: As cold spurs U.S. soy crop concern, no threat yet.
newsitem.headline: As cold spurs U.S. soy crop concern, no threat yet.

text.p: The record-breaking cold temperatures seen in the U.S. Midwest this week have generated concerns about soybean growth and germination rates, but no developmental problems have been noted yet, agronomists and crop watchers said.
"In terms of soybeans, it's a waiting game," said Dr. Ellsworth Christmas, agronomist with Purdue University in West Lafayette, Ind. "There are no problems so far."
Although there are no overt signs of damage, farmers are nervously eyeing forecasts for frost in some northern Corn Belt states Thursday night, cash grain sources said.
"We're supposed to see record cold in the Quad Cities tonight, and that is going to zap the beans that are out of the ground," said one grain merchandiser in east-central Iowa.
Overnight lows are forecast to dip below freezing across the northern half of Illinois and Indiana and most of Ohio, according to U.S. forecasters.
Because most of the U.S. soybean crop has either just been planted or is yet to be planted, only a handful of soybean acres will be susceptible to any frost damage.
According to Monday's crop progress report from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, only two percent of Ohio's soybean crop had emerged as of Sunday.
Emergence data from other states were unvailable, but grain merchandisers throughout the Corn Belt reported scattered instances of emerged plants.
The soybeans that have been planted will escape damage if the weather in the Midwest warms significantly and becomes much drier in areas where soils are saturated, agronomists said.
"We could end up with a near-normal population of soybeans or we could end up with a near 100 percent loss or anything in between," Christmas said.
"It's going to depend on what happens with the weather in the next few days," he said.
Warmer temperatures will speed the development of the growing soybeans while drier soil is needed in some areas to guard against the possibility of seed rot, Christmas said.
Soybeans--especially those with cracked seed coatings-- planted in cool, moist soil are more susceptible to rot organisms, Christmas said.
Saturated soils and cold temperatures were more prevalent in the eastern Corn Belt, and some crop observers reported more favorable growing conditions in the West.
"In northern Iowa, the beans are still in the bag, so they aren't susceptible to cold weather," said Mark Carlton, crop specialist for Iowa State University.
"As you get further north, the soils are drier so there is less of a problem (with seed rot)," he said.
Most U.S. meteorolgists expect the Midwest and U.S. Central Plains to warm up this weekend and see a return to more seasonble temperatures next week.
"We feel pretty confident this will be the last cold weather threat in the Midwest," said Craig Solberg, meteorologist with Freese-Notis Weather, in Des Moines, Iowa.
